notes:
Relations

  • A relation $R$ on set $A$ is a subset of $A\times A$.
  • Reflexive: $(a,a)\in R\ \forall a\in A$. Symmetric: $(a,b)\in R\Rightarrow(b,a)\in R$. Transitive: $(a,b),(b,c)\in R\Rightarrow(a,c)\in R$.
  • Equivalence relation: reflexive + symmetric + transitive. It partitions $A$ into disjoint equivalence classes.

Functions: one-one, onto

  • One-one (injective): distinct inputs give distinct outputs, i.e. $f(x_1)=f(x_2)\Rightarrow x_1=x_2$.
  • Onto (surjective): every element of codomain has a pre-image, i.e. range = codomain.
  • Bijective: one-one and onto — only bijections are invertible.
  • If $f:A\to B$ with $n(A)=m$, $n(B)=n$: number of one-one functions $=\ ^nP_m$ (needs $m\le n$); number of functions $=n^m$.
TypeTest
One-oneHorizontal line cuts graph at most once
OntoEvery horizontal line (within codomain) cuts graph at least once

Composition of functions

  • $(gof)(x)=g(f(x))$. Composition is associative but generally not commutative.
  • If $f,g$ are both one-one (onto), $gof$ is one-one (onto).

Invertible functions

  • $f$ is invertible $\iff$ $f$ is bijective. Then $f^{-1}of=I_A$ and $fof^{-1}=I_B$.
  • If $f:A\to B,\ g:B\to C$ are invertible, then $(gof)^{-1}=f^{-1}og^{-1}$.

Binary operations

  • A binary operation $*$ on set $A$ is a function $*:A\times A\to A$, i.e. $A$ is closed under $*$.
  • Commutative: $a*b=b*a$. Associative: $(a*b)*c=a*(b*c)$.
  • Identity element $e$: $a*e=e*a=a$ (unique if it exists).
  • Inverse of $a$: element $b$ with $a*b=b*a=e$.
  • Usual $+,\times$ on $\mathbb{R}$ are commutative & associative; identity $0$ and $1$ respectively. Subtraction and division are neither commutative nor associative.

Exam tip

KCET usually asks 2 questions from this chapter — one on identifying reflexive/symmetric/transitive or counting equivalence relations, and one on checking one-one/onto or evaluating a binary operation's identity/inverse. Learn to test properties on small finite sets quickly by writing out ordered pairs.

questions.q: Let $R=\{(a,b): a\le b\}$ be a relation on the set of real numbers. $R$ is
options: reflexive and transitive but not symmetric
symmetric and transitive but not reflexive
questions.explanation: $a\le a$ (reflexive); $a\le b, b\le c \Rightarrow a\le c$ (transitive); but $a\le b$ does not imply $b\le a$, so not symmetric.
questions.trick: $\le$ is reflexive+transitive but $a\le b$ never forces $b\le a$.

questions.explanation: All $(a,a)$ present (reflexive); $(1,2),(2,1)$ both present (symmetric); $(1,2),(2,1)\Rightarrow(1,1)$ present, no other chain needed (transitive). Hence equivalence relation.
questions.trick: List all pairs and check R, S, T directly on the finite set.

questions.q: The number of equivalence relations on the set $\{1,2,3\}$ containing $(1,2)$ and $(2,1)$ is
questions.explanation: Since $1$ and $2$ must be in the same class, the partitions are $\{1,2,3\}$ (all together) or $\{1,2\},\{3\}$ — exactly 2 equivalence relations.
questions.trick: Fixing $1\sim2$ leaves only two possible partitions of the set.

questions.q: Let $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be defined by $f(x)=3x-5$. Then $f$ is
questions.explanation: $f$ is linear with nonzero slope so it is injective; for any $y\in\mathbb{R}$, $x=(y+5)/3$ gives $f(x)=y$, so it is surjective too.
questions.trick: Linear $f$ with nonzero slope is automatically bijective on $\mathbb{R}$.

questions.q: The function $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ given by $f(x)=x^2$ is
questions.explanation: $f(-2)=f(2)=4$ so not one-one; negative numbers have no pre-image (since $x^2\ge 0$), so not onto.
questions.trick: $x^2$: $f(-a)=f(a)$ kills one-one; negatives unreached kills onto.

questions.q: If $f:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ is defined by $f(x)=x^2$, then $f$ is
questions.explanation: On $\mathbb{N}$, $x_1^2=x_2^2\Rightarrow x_1=x_2$ (both positive), so one-one. But $2\in\mathbb{N}$ has no pre-image since $\sqrt2\notin\mathbb{N}$, so not onto.
questions.trick: On $\mathbb{N}$, $x^2$ is one-one (no negatives) but skips non-squares.

questions.q: Let $f:A\to B$ where $n(A)=4$ and $n(B)=3$. The number of one-one functions from $A$ to $B$ is
questions.explanation: A one-one function requires $n(A)\le n(B)$. Since $4>3$, no one-one function exists.
questions.trick: One-one needs $n(A)\le n(B)$; here $4>3$ so the count is $0$.

questions.q: If $A=\{1,2,3\}$ and $B=\{4,5\}$, the number of onto functions from $A$ to $B$ is
questions.explanation: Total functions $=2^3=8$; subtract the 2 constant (not onto) functions: $8-2=6$.
questions.trick: Onto count $=$ total functions $n^m$ minus the constant (non-onto) ones.

questions.q: If $f(x)=2x+3$ and $g(x)=x^2$, then $(gof)(1)$ equals
questions.trick: Composition: evaluate the inner function first, then the outer.

questions.q: If $f(x)=x+2$ and $g(x)=2x-3$, then $(fog)(x)-(gof)(x)$ equals
questions.trick: Compute $fog$ and $gof$ separately, then subtract term by term.

questions.q: The inverse of $f(x)=\dfrac{2x-1}{3}$ (as a function on $\mathbb{R}$) is
questions.explanation: Let $y=(2x-1)/3\Rightarrow 3y=2x-1\Rightarrow x=(3y+1)/2$. So $f^{-1}(x)=(3x+1)/2$.
questions.trick: Swap $x,y$ in $y=f(x)$ and solve for $y$ to get $f^{-1}$.

questions.q: If $f:A\to B$ and $g:B\to C$ are both bijections, then $(gof)^{-1}$ equals
questions.explanation: Standard result: the inverse of a composition reverses the order, $(gof)^{-1}=f^{-1}og^{-1}$.
questions.trick: Inverse of a composite reverses order: $(gof)^{-1}=f^{-1}og^{-1}$.

questions.q: A binary operation $*$ is defined on $\mathbb{Z}$ by $a*b=a+b-ab$. The identity element for $*$ is
questions.explanation: Need $a*e=a\Rightarrow a+e-ae=a\Rightarrow e(1-a)=0$ for all $a$, so $e=0$. Check: $a*0=a+0-0=a$. Identity is 0.
questions.trick: Set $a*e=a$ for all $a$ and solve for $e$ to find the identity.

questions.q: On $\mathbb{Q}$, the operation $a*b=\dfrac{ab}{2}$ is
questions.explanation: $a*b=ab/2=ba/2=b*a$ (commutative). $(a*b)*c=(ab/2)*c=abc/4$ and $a*(b*c)=a*(bc/2)=abc/4$, equal (associative).
questions.trick: Check $a*b=b*a$ for commutative, expand both groupings for associative.

questions.q: Let $R$ be the relation on $\mathbb{Z}$ given by $aRb$ if $a-b$ is divisible by 5. This relation is
questions.explanation: $a-a=0$ divisible by 5 (reflexive); $a-b$ divisible $\Rightarrow b-a=-(a-b)$ divisible (symmetric); $a-b,b-c$ divisible $\Rightarrow a-c=(a-b)+(b-c)$ divisible (transitive). Equivalence relation.
questions.trick: Divisibility-by-$k$ relations are always reflexive, symmetric, transitive.

questions.q: If $A=\{1,2,3,\dots,n\}$, the total number of relations that can be defined on $A$ is
questions.explanation: A relation is any subset of $A\times A$, which has $n^2$ elements, giving $2^{n^2}$ subsets.
questions.trick: Relations = subsets of $A\times A$ ($n^2$ pairs), so count is $2^{n^2}$.

questions.q: The relation $R=\{(a,b): |a-b|\le 2\}$ on $\mathbb{Z}$ is
options: reflexive and symmetric but not transitive
questions.explanation: $|a-a|=0\le2$ (reflexive); $|a-b|=|b-a|$ (symmetric); but take $a=1,b=3,c=5$: $|1-3|=2$, $|3-5|=2$, yet $|1-5|=4>2$, so not transitive.
questions.trick: Find one counterexample chain (small numbers) to kill transitivity fast.

questions.q: If $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ is defined by $f(x)=|x|$, then $f$ is
questions.explanation: $f(-1)=f(1)=1$ so not one-one; negative reals are never attained, so not onto.
questions.trick: $|x|$ is even ($f(-x)=f(x)$) so never one-one; negatives never hit.

questions.q: On the set of natural numbers, the binary operation $*$ given by $a*b=\text{HCF}(a,b)$ is
questions.explanation: $\text{HCF}(a,b)=\text{HCF}(b,a)$ (commutative) and $\text{HCF}(\text{HCF}(a,b),c)=\text{HCF}(a,\text{HCF}(b,c))$ (associative).
questions.trick: HCF/GCD/LCM operations are always commutative and associative.

questions.q: Let $f:\{1,2,3\}\to\{1,2,3\}$ be defined by $f(1)=2,\ f(2)=3,\ f(3)=1$. Then $f^{-1}$ is given by
questions.explanation: $f$ is a bijection (a 3-cycle), so it is invertible. Since $f(1)=2$, $f^{-1}(2)=1$; since $f(2)=3$, $f^{-1}(3)=2$; since $f(3)=1$, $f^{-1}(1)=3$.
questions.trick: Read the mapping backward: $f(a)=b\Rightarrow f^{-1}(b)=a$.

questions.explanation: Every element relates to itself (reflexive); $(1,2),(2,1)$ pair symmetrically; and $(1,2),(2,1)\Rightarrow(1,1)$ holds, so it is transitive too. Hence an equivalence relation.
questions.trick: Verify reflexive, symmetric, transitive directly from the listed pairs.

questions.q: The relation $R$ on $\mathbb{N}$ defined by $aRb$ if $a$ divides $b$ is
options: reflexive and transitive but not symmetric
questions.explanation: Every $a$ divides itself (reflexive); if $a|b$ and $b|c$ then $a|c$ (transitive); but $2|4$ does not mean $4|2$, so not symmetric.
questions.trick: 'Divides' is reflexive and transitive, but $2|4$ does not give $4|2$.

questions.q: Let $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be defined by $f(x)=x^3$. Then $f$ is
questions.explanation: $x^3$ is strictly increasing so it is one-one, and as $x$ ranges over $\mathbb{R}$, $x^3$ takes every real value, so it is onto.
questions.trick: Odd-power monomials $x^{2k+1}$ are always bijections on $\mathbb{R}$.

questions.q: If $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ is given by $f(x)=5-x$, then $f$ is
options: not invertible since it is not one-one
not invertible since it is not onto
questions.explanation: $f$ is a bijection on $\mathbb{R}$ (strictly decreasing, covers all reals). Setting $y=5-x$ gives $x=5-y$, so $f^{-1}(x)=5-x$, i.e. $f$ is its own inverse.
questions.trick: Self-inverse check: solve $y=f(x)$ for $x$; same form means $f=f^{-1}$.

questions.q: Let $A=\{1,2,3\}$ and $B=\{1,2,3,4\}$. The number of one-one functions from $A$ to $B$ is
questions.explanation: Number of one-one functions $=\ ^4P_3=4\times3\times2=24$.
questions.trick: Count one-one functions with permutations: $^{n(B)}P_{n(A)}$.

questions.q: If $f(x)=x^2+1$ and $g(x)=x-1$, then $(fog)(3)$ equals
questions.trick: Innermost first: find $g(3)$, then apply $f$ to that result.

questions.q: For $f(x)=2x+1$ and $g(x)=\dfrac{x-1}{2}$, which of the following is correct?
options: $f$ and $g$ have the same domain restriction
questions.trick: Confirm $f(g(x))=x$ and $g(f(x))=x$ to identify an inverse pair.

questions.q: A binary operation $*$ on $\mathbb{R}$ is defined by $a*b=a+b+ab$. The inverse of an element $a\ (a\ne -1)$ is
questions.explanation: Identity element $e=0$ since $a*0=a$. Solve $a*b=0$: $a+b+ab=0\Rightarrow b(1+a)=-a\Rightarrow b=\dfrac{-a}{1+a}$.
questions.trick: Find the identity first, then solve $a*b=e$ for $b$ to get the inverse.

questions.q: Which of the following statements is INCORRECT?
options: Every one-one function from a finite set to itself is onto
Composition of two one-one functions is one-one
Every onto function from a finite set to itself is one-one but need not be invertible
Composition of two onto functions is onto
questions.explanation: On a finite set, an onto function to itself is automatically one-one and hence bijective, so it IS invertible — making option C (which claims it need not be invertible) the false statement.
questions.trick: On a finite set: one-one $\iff$ onto $\iff$ bijective $\iff$ invertible.

questions.q: Let $R$ be a relation on the set of triangles in a plane defined as $R=\{(T_1,T_2): T_1 \text{ is similar to } T_2\}$. Then $R$ is
questions.explanation: Similarity of triangles is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive, so it is an equivalence relation.
questions.trick: Similarity/congruence of shapes is always an equivalence relation.

questions.q: If $A=\{1,2,3\}$, the number of relations on $A$ that are reflexive is
questions.explanation: $A\times A$ has 9 pairs; the 3 diagonal pairs must be included (fixed), and each of the remaining $9-3=6$ pairs is free, giving $2^6$ reflexive relations.
questions.trick: Reflexive relations: diagonal fixed, remaining $n^2-n$ pairs free $\Rightarrow2^{n^2-n}$.

questions.q: The relation $R=\{(a,b): a,b \in \mathbb{Z}, a-b \text{ is an integer}\}$ on $\mathbb{Z}$ is
questions.explanation: For any integers $a,b$, $a-b$ is always an integer, so every pair is related — this makes $R=\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}$, which is trivially reflexive, symmetric and transitive.
questions.trick: If every pair satisfies the condition, $R=A\times A$, trivially an equivalence.

questions.q: If $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$, $f(x)=\dfrac{x}{x^2+1}$, then $f$ is
questions.explanation: $f(2)=\dfrac{2}{5}$ and $f(1/2)=\dfrac{1/2}{5/4}=\dfrac{2}{5}$, so $f$ is not one-one. Also the range of $f$ is $[-1/2,1/2]$, not all of $\mathbb{R}$, so not onto.
questions.trick: Test $f(a)=f(1/a)$ to catch non-one-one; find the range to test onto.

questions.q: On $\mathbb{N}$, define $a*b=a^b$. Which property fails for $*$?
questions.explanation: $2*3=8$ but $3*2=9$, so it is not commutative; also $(2*2)*3=4^3=64$ but $2*(2*3)=2^8=256$, so not associative either. It is closed since $a^b\in\mathbb{N}$.
questions.trick: Try small numbers like $2,3$ to disprove commutativity and associativity fast.
Read the mapping in reverse: $f(3)=4\Rightarrow f^{-1}(4)=3$.

questions.q: Assertion (A): The identity relation on a set $A$ is always an equivalence relation. Reason (R): The identity relation is reflexive, symmetric and transitive. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, R is false
A is false, R is true
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
questions.explanation: The identity relation $\{(a,a):a\in A\}$ trivially satisfies all three properties, so both A and R are true and R correctly explains A.
questions.trick: Identity relation $\{(a,a)\}$ trivially satisfies R, S, T — always equivalence.

questions.q: If $n(A)=3$, the total number of binary operations that can be defined on $A$ is
questions.explanation: A binary operation is a function from $A\times A$ (9 elements) to $A$ (3 choices each), giving $3^9$ possible binary operations.
questions.trick: Binary operations on a set of size $n$: total $n^{n^2}$ (functions $A\times A\to A$).

questions.q: Let $f(x)=\sin x$ restricted to $\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$ with codomain $[-1,1]$. Then $f$ is
questions.explanation: On $\left[-\pi/2,\pi/2\right]$, $\sin x$ is strictly increasing (one-one) and its range is exactly $[-1,1]$ (onto), so it is a bijection — this is the basis for defining $\sin^{-1}x$.
questions.trick: $\sin x$ on $[-\pi/2,\pi/2]$ is strictly increasing with range $[-1,1]$ — a bijection.

questions.q: If $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ is defined by $f(x)=\begin{cases}2x, & x>0\\0, & x\le 0\end{cases}$, then $f$ is
questions.explanation: Every $x\le 0$ maps to $0$, so $f(-1)=f(-2)=0$ shows $f$ is not one-one. For $x>0$, $f(x)=2x>0$, and for $x\le0$, $f(x)=0$; so the range is $[0,\infty)$ and every negative real is never attained, so $f$ is not onto either.
questions.trick: A whole region collapsing to one value kills one-one; an unreached codomain part kills onto.

questions.q: On the set of all functions from $\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$, if $*$ is composition of functions, which is true?
options: $*$ is associative but not commutative in general
questions.explanation: Function composition always satisfies $(f\circ g)\circ h=f\circ(g\circ h)$ (associative), but in general $f\circ g\ne g\circ f$ (not commutative), e.g. $f(x)=x+1,g(x)=x^2$.
questions.trick: Function composition is always associative, but rarely commutative.
